images.prompt: Photorealistic macro photograph of a handcrafted miniature tabletop diorama. A long brushed graphite day strip about the length of a forearm runs left to right across a pale neutral tabletop, with shallow slots along its top edge. Near the left end sits one small ivory paper chip, folded into a tight concertina no wider than a matchbox, its pleats crisp and even. An acid-lime tab on its leading end marks the short call that was booked. Further along the strip, a frosted acrylic lunch block and two ivory focus blocks sit in their slots, evenly spaced with open gaps between them. A graphite end stop caps the right end. Fine paper fibres show along the chip's folds, and light dust sits in the empty slots. The day looks open and uncluttered. Wide 16:9 landscape frame. The hero object sits slightly left of centre on the lower third, with the related objects extending to the right so the workflow reads left to right. Clean, generous negative space above. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Materials are limited and tactile: heavyweight ivory cotton paper and card with visible fibres, soft folds and slightly deckled edges; matte, bead-blasted graphite metal with fine machining lines, chamfered edges and tiny hex fasteners; frosted acrylic with milky edges and a soft internal glow; sandblasted frosted glass. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Colour palette is restrained and nearly monochrome: white #FFFFFF, warm ivory, pale neutral #F3F5F2, soft grey-green #DCE1DA, muted graphite #626A64 and deep graphite #191D1B. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: one large soft key light from the upper left at about 45 degrees, like diffused north-window daylight, with a gentle white bounce fill from the right; soft grounded contact shadows fall to the lower right. Camera: 100mm macro lens at f/4, eye level with the tabletop, three-quarter view. The hero object is tack sharp and the background melts into smooth, creamy blur on a seamless pale neutral sweep. Mood: calm, precise, orderly and quietly premium, like high-end editorial product photography. Strictly no people, figures, faces, hands or silhouettes. No readable text, letters, numbers, clock digits, logos, signage or user-interface graphics anywhere. No holograms, floating screens, robots with faces, dense cable tangles, carnival or circus elements, cartoon or plastic CGI look, oversaturated colour, lens flare or heavy vignette.

Photorealistic macro photograph of a handcrafted miniature tabletop diorama, captured mid-disaster. The same concertina chip has unfolded along the entire day strip. Its pleats have opened into a long zigzag of ivory paper that fills every slot, rising and sagging as it goes. As it expanded it shoved the frosted lunch block and both focus blocks to the right, where they are piled against the graphite end stop; one focus block has flipped over, and the lunch block is caught mid-fall over the side of the strip. The acid-lime tab is still at the leading edge of the unfolding paper, pressed hard against the pile. Loose pleats bow upward, a torn corner flutters in the air, and creases and paper dust along the strip lead back to the chip's starting slot. Wide 16:9 landscape frame, same layout and angle as the calm version of this scene. The hero object stays slightly left of centre, and the spread of the disaster runs to the right and toward the camera so its path can be traced back to the source. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Materials are limited and tactile: heavyweight ivory cotton paper and card with visible fibres, soft folds and slightly deckled edges; matte, bead-blasted graphite metal with fine machining lines, chamfered edges and tiny hex fasteners; frosted acrylic with milky edges and a soft internal glow; sandblasted frosted glass. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: the same soft upper-left key and right-side bounce fill as a calm studio setup, unchanged, so the disorder reads as physical and real rather than theatrical. Airborne paper, grains and fragments catch the key light with crisp edge highlights. Camera: 85mm lens at f/5.6, same three-quarter tabletop angle, fast shutter freezing everything mid-air. Focus sits where the chain reaction started, and the spread softens into the depth of field. Mood: absurd but plausible, an orderly system that got out of hand, still clean and editorial. Photorealistic photograph of a vast handcrafted miniature landscape diorama. A range of low terraced hills rolls to a hazy horizon, every slope formed from vast weathered pleats of ivory paper, stiffened and greyed at the folds, with scrub growing in the creases. At the far end, the graphite day strip lies as a long broken ridge wall, and the lunch and focus blocks are tumbled boulders the size of houses, cracked and bleached, heaped against the end stop. Wind has frayed the pleat edges into fibrous fringes. On the nearest slope, a slim graphite cutter rig runs on a short rail, slicing the unfolded paper into clean, even segments with a lime wire blade and stacking each section on a lime-edged pallet; the first recovered short block sits squarely in its own restored slot. Wide 16:9 panoramic frame. The main ruin anchors the left or centre foreground, terrain rolls back to a distant horizon on the upper third, and the lime recovery rig sits in the right midground. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents.
